behavior_items: The reproducer targets GCC's x86-64 machine description pattern `*tls_global_dynamic_64_<mode>`, which implements the global-dynamic thread-local storage access sequence used when the address of a TLS symbol must be resolved at run time through `__tls_get_addr`.

Semantically, the RTL pattern claims only two visible effects: it sets the result register operand 0, constrained to `%rax`, to the return value of a call, and it performs an `UNSPEC_TLS_GD` operation using the TLS symbol and stack pointer. No explicit clobber of `%rdi` is described in the pattern.

The output template emitted by the pattern tells a different story from the RTL. Before the call, GCC emits `lea ...@tlsgd(%rip), %rdi`, which materializes the TLS descriptor argument in `%rdi`. That instruction overwrites `%rdi` unconditionally, so `%rdi` is an implicit input/output side effect of the insn sequence.

On x86-64 SysV, `%rdi` is the first integer argument register and is caller-saved. In the TLS global-dynamic ABI sequence, `%rdi` is specifically used to pass the TLS descriptor to `__tls_get_addr`. Because the backend pattern omits `%rdi` from its clobber list, the register allocator and dataflow passes may incorrectly assume that any live value already held in `%rdi` survives this insn.

The emitted sequence also adds TLS-specific instruction prefixes: `data16` on non-x32 targets to preserve correct debug `.loc` behavior, then either another `0x66`/`0x6666` prefix plus `rex64`, followed by a direct or GOT-based call form depending on assembler and PLT configuration. These prefixes are not the bug; they are part of the required ABI/call sequence around `__tls_get_addr`.

The core compiler-behavior defect is therefore a mismatch between RTL semantics and final assembly semantics: the machine description models only the call result in `%rax`, while the emitted assembly additionally destroys `%rdi`. GCC optimization and register allocation rely on RTL, not printed assembly, so they can make invalid liveness decisions.

A practical failure mode is that GCC may keep some unrelated program value live in `%rdi` across a TLS global-dynamic access, then later reuse that supposedly preserved value. After expansion, `%rdi` actually contains the TLS descriptor address or other transient call setup state, so subsequent code observes corrupted data, leading to miscompilation.

The bug is especially subtle because ordinary calls already clobber caller-saved registers, but here the problematic overwrite happens in the hand-written `lea` that is part of the single `define_insn` expansion. If `%rdi` is not represented as a call-clobbered operand or explicit clobber in the pattern, GCC cannot reason correctly about the pre-call register overwrite performed by that `lea`.

The same reasoning applies to the closely related local-dynamic TLS patterns mentioned by the bug title: any backend pattern that emits `lea ... , %rdi` as part of the TLS resolver setup must model `%rdi` as clobbered or otherwise consumed so that reload/LRA and later optimizers do not treat it as preserved.

In short, the reproducer exercises backend correctness rather than front-end language semantics: it demonstrates that the x86 TLS dynamic access pattern's printed assembly uses `%rdi` implicitly, but the RTL contract exposed to GCC middle-end and backend analyses omits that side effect, enabling wrong-code generation.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer highlights an x86-64 GCC backend bug in the TLS global-dynamic/local-dynamic machine description patterns. The RTL says the insn only produces a result in `%rax` via a call, but the emitted assembly first executes `lea ...@tlsgd(%rip), %rdi`, which overwrites `%rdi` to pass the TLS descriptor to `__tls_get_addr`. Because `%rdi` is not modeled as a clobber or operand, GCC can incorrectly keep live values there across the TLS access, causing register-liveness mistakes and miscompilation. The failure is a backend RTL-versus-assembly side-effect mismatch, not an issue with the TLS prefixes or call sequence themselves.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a backend machine-description insn whose RTL contract under-specifies the real effects of the emitted assembly. Here, the x86-64 TLS global-dynamic/local-dynamic patterns model a call returning in `%rax`, but the output template also emits `lea ... , %rdi` before the call. That means the instruction sequence has an extra hard-register side effect on `%rdi` that is invisible to RTL-based liveness, reload/LRA, scheduling, and dataflow analysis. The failure therefore matches a classic GCC backend defect class: mismatch between `define_insn` semantics and the actual assembler printed by the output template. Because `%rdi` is the SysV ABI argument register used to pass the TLS descriptor to `__tls_get_addr`, omitting it from operands/clobbers can let GCC keep unrelated live values in `%rdi` across the TLS access and later reuse a register value that was in fact destroyed. The same pattern likely affects both global-dynamic and local-dynamic TLS forms if they emit the same `%rdi` setup sequence.
possible_causes: Missing explicit `%rdi` clobber in the x86 backend `define_insn` for `*tls_global_dynamic_64_<mode>` despite the emitted `lea ... , %rdi` overwriting that hard register.

Incorrect RTL modeling of the TLS dynamic access sequence as only a call result in `%rax` plus `UNSPEC_TLS_GD`, instead of modeling `%rdi` as an input/output or early clobber hard register used for `__tls_get_addr` argument setup.

Parallel defect in the related `*tls_local_dynamic_64_<mode>` pattern or any shared helper pattern that also emits `lea ... , %rdi` without advertising the side effect to register allocation/dataflow.

Backend call/TLS pattern design bug where pre-call setup done inside a handwritten asm template is not represented in RTL, causing reload/LRA and liveness passes to assume `%rdi` survives until the modeled call semantics apply.

Possible omission in x86 MD constraints or call-used register annotations specific to these TLS patterns, so GCC does not treat `%rdi` as consumed/clobbered at the point of the insn sequence even though the ABI-mandated TLS resolver setup requires it.
evidence: The pattern output explicitly emits `lea{q} ... , %rdi`, which unconditionally overwrites `%rdi` before the call.
The RTL for the shown `define_insn` contains no `%rdi` operand and no `(clobber (reg:P DI_REG))`, so the destructive effect is absent from GCC's internal semantics.

The bug report and behavior analysis both identify the issue as an implicit `%rdi` clobber in `*tls_(local|global)_dynamic_64_<mode>`, indicating the problem is in GCC production compiler backend code, not the reproducer.

`%rdi` is the SysV first integer argument register and is specifically used here to pass the TLS descriptor to `__tls_get_addr`, making the pre-call overwrite architecturally required and therefore something the RTL must model.

The observed failure mode is consistent with wrong-code from stale liveness assumptions: GCC may preserve a value in `%rdi` across the TLS access according to RTL, while the printed assembly has already destroyed it.

In both case, this function returns the number of "spare" bits. For example, if two quantities for which this function returns at least 1 are added, the addition is known not to overflow.
